citeAs: Conneau, A., Ma, M., Khanuja, S., Zhang, Y., Axelrod, V., Dalmia, S., Riesa, J., Rivera, C., Bapna, A. (2022). FLEURS: Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech. arXiv:2205.12446.
creator: Alexis Conneau, Min Ma, Simran Khanuja, Yu Zhang, Vera Axelrod, Siddharth Dalmia, Jason Riesa, Clara Rivera, Ankur Bapna (Meta AI Research, Google Research, Carnegie Mellon University)
description: FLEURS (Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech) is an n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language. It contains natural human speech and high quality transcripts, and can be used for a variety of speech tasks including Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification, Translation, and Retrieval.

name: FLEURS
rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 (three recordings per sentence by three different native speakers)
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three recordings per sentence were collected from three different native speakers. After recording, each recording was evaluated by additional workers to assess whether the recording corresponds to the input sentence. Invalid recordings were discarded. A sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% was imposed when possible.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset imposes a sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible. Speakers are different between train and dev/test sets to avoid over-fitting on speaker ID for the LangID task. The dataset covers 17 language families and 27 unique writing systems, with geographic groupings. Performance gaps across geographical groups are noted, with Western European languages benefiting from larger amounts of unlabeled pre-training data. The dataset is built on Wikipedia-sourced sentences, which may introduce domain bias.
rai:dataCollection: Data collection started from the FLoRes-101 dataset, which contains 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia translated into 101 languages by human translators. Only the dev and devtest sets (2009 sentences total) were used, as the test set was not publicly available. These were re-split into train (1509), dev (150), and test (350) sentences. For each sentence in 102 languages, three recordings were collected from three different native speakers, with a sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% imposed when possible. Each recording was then evaluated by additional workers to assess whether it corresponds to the input sentence; invalid recordings were discarded. The speech sampling rate is 16kHz, and all segments are within 30 seconds. Train/dev and test sets have disjoint speakers, with a target ratio of 7:1:2.
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In the first version of the dataset, about 21.5% of the sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. The authors plan to fill these gaps in future versions of the dataset.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data is the FLoRes-101 machine translation benchmark, which contains 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into 101 languages by human translators. The dev and devtest splits (2009 sentences) were used as the basis for speech recording.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: In the first version of the dataset, about 21.5% of the sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. All recordings are kept as-is from either quiet or noisy environments, without any data augmentations. The dataset is built on FLoRes-101 sentences from English Wikipedia, which may not cover all domains equally. Results show significant performance gaps across geographical groups, with Sub-Saharan African and South Asian languages performing worse than Western European languages, partly due to limited unlabeled data availability.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For textual data, transcripts from FLoRes-101 human translators were reused. NFC and then FST normalization was applied to each sentence, followed by lower-casing, normalization and removal of punctuations. Words were split into characters, with a token for word boundaries. Three versions of each sentence are provided: the original raw transcript (SRC_RAW), the preprocessed version (SRC_NORM), and its character-based version (SRC_CHAR). A universal vocabulary of characters was adopted as the modeling and evaluation unit.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors plan to fill missing data gaps (approximately 21.5% of sentences missing in the first version) in future versions of the dataset.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The goal of FLEURS is to enable speech technology in more languages and catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding. The authors hope the dataset will catalyze research towards building massively multilingual speech and text representations, enabling progress towards building speech technologies for everyone.
rai:dataUseCases: FLEURS is intended for evaluating speech technology across a variety of tasks including: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Speech-to-Text and Speech-to-Speech Translation, and Multilingual Speech-to-Speech and Speech-to-Text Retrieval. It is particularly suited for evaluating data-efficient multilingual pre-trained representations of speech and text, and for catalyzing research in few-shot understanding in many languages, especially low-resource ones.
